title: Lecture 10. Experiment
summary:
Ancient Greeks sought truth. First, they formulated rules of reasoning leading to truth. Then they began to doubt "obvious" things and started relying on observation results as proof of truth. But over time, philosophers realized that observation results alone were also insufficient: to find truth, one needed not just observations, but observations that precisely define the connection between phenomena. And the search for such procedures led to the creation of the main scientific method — the experiment, the meaning of which lies in controlling all factors of the observed phenomenon.

As we discussed in the first lesson of the module, the purpose of any research is first to build a theoretical model, and then to test its correspondence to reality. Correspondence to reality is determined by how fully and accurately we were able to identify the factors of our model. And the very logic of the experiment is aimed at testing hypotheses, that is, testing the strength of the connection between our subject of study and its factors. The stronger these connections, the stronger the predictive value of the model.

The first and most obvious criterion for a connection between two phenomena is their temporal relationship. If one event repeatedly occurs immediately after another, it means these events are somehow related, and one follows from the other. For example, after we throw a stone into the water, ripples always appear, meaning the thrown stone, and only it, is the cause of the disturbances on the water.

Such an experimental design is called "before-after". It consists of the following. First, we observe the calm surface of the water. Then we act upon it — we throw a stone. After which, we observe changes — ripples on the water. From this, we conclude that between the state of calm and disturbance, one and only one! event occurred — the falling of the stone. This means that this one event was the factor that changed the state of the water.

Applying this logic to an example closer to our topic — the effectiveness of medicines was tested in the same way for centuries. A patient was observed before taking the medicine and after. And the conclusion was drawn that if the patient felt better, then the medicine worked. But here a question arises: what if other factors, which we cannot control, influenced the patient? What if the improvement occurred not as a result of taking the medicine at all, but for some other reasons that we do not take into account? How can these other factors be excluded from observation?

In response to these questions, the next step in the development of experimental methodology was that the experiment needed to be repeated many times. And if the patient felt better each time, then it was the action of the medicine, and not something else. And this is good logic for physical or technical systems, for example, with a stone thrown into water, where the experiment can be reproduced exactly the same as the previous one. But with people, this won't work: "you can't step into the same river twice" and reproduce exactly the same experience with the same person, because a person is constantly changing, at least under the influence of previous experimental experience. Behavior is too complex an object.

And then a crucial step was made in the development of the experimental procedure, which is called a controlled study, that is, an experiment using a control group. Its essence is to take two IDENTICAL objects of study, only act upon one of them — the experimental object, and then compare it with the second — the control object, which we did not act upon. In this way, we "separate" the influence of our intervention, for example, a medicine, from all other factors. BUT! on one condition, that the experimental and control observation objects are indeed identical.

In physical systems, achieving identity is easy. One can find or make two strictly identical stones and throw them into the water in exactly the same way. But people, as already mentioned, are too complex an object. It is impossible to find two identical people. Therefore, the next important step was taken: groups of people began to be compared, and to ensure the identity of these groups — experimental and control — a simple method was devised, which received the name randomization.

Randomization (or ensuring randomness) consists of distributing people into these two groups — experimental and control — strictly randomly. The randomness of selection "balances" both known and unknown factors influencing the subjects. The main thing is that the randomization method, even theoretically, could not be linked to any factors whatsoever. For example, one can assign numbers to all people participating in the study, and then use a random number generator to divide them into two groups. Such studies are called randomized controlled trials (RCTs). And this research method has the highest degree of reliability compared to all others.

The above is the main thing to know about the experimental procedure. However, its subsequent modifications, called "blind" studies using a fictitious medicine – placebo, can also be mentioned:

Single-blind – the patient does not know which treatment they have been assigned, but the doctor does. Participants in the control group, like participants in the experimental group, are also given medicine, but it is a placebo – without any active substance. At the same time, the participants in both groups think they are receiving real medicine. The necessity of this step was due to the fact that the outcome of the investigated drug's action could be influenced by the mindset of patients who know whether they are receiving treatment or not. Double-blind — neither the doctor nor the patient knows the assigned therapy. This helps to exclude the voluntary or involuntary influence of the doctor on the course of treatment for specific patients. Triple-blind — neither the doctor, nor the patient, nor those who organize the study and process the data know the assigned therapy for a specific patient — whether it is a real medicine or a placebo. In such a case, the staff only has a list of patient codes and a list of medicine codes. The list of patients indicating their belonging to the experimental or control group, and the list indicating drug codes, are kept secret from everyone. At the very beginning of the study, they are placed in a safe and opened only at the final stage of processing the research results.

Not as strict as in drug trials, but still following the logic of the same experimental procedure described above, studies are also conducted to evaluate the results of preventive programs. For example, in an educational organization where certain classes participate in a preventive program (essentially becoming an experimental group), the control group can be classes from the same school that did not participate in the preventive program, with the caveat that they are identical in age, profile, and other parameters. Similarly, a comparison can be made between educational organizations that participated and did not participate in a certain preventive program.
